title: ⭐⭐ Revision: the ladder, the budget and the plate

questions.prompt: A school is printing its new report card. The subjects are gathered under headings: one heading has to stand above English, German and Spanish, and the second above biology, chemistry and physics. Which two headings does the school print, in that order?

options.text: Spanish, and then chemistry
The sciences, and then languages
Language, and then science
Languages, and then the sciences

questions.explanation: A heading has to cover every subject standing under it, and that is why both of these words name a whole group instead of one line inside it, and why both come out plural: one gathers the tongues a pupil learns, the other the subjects that study matter and living things. Printing a single subject there answers a far smaller question than the report card asked. Swapping the two headings round is just as wrong, since it would file German with the laboratories. And watch what goes under neither of them: geometry is a branch of maths, and art belongs to no heading at all.

questions.prompt: A college secretary sorts two applications by how far each candidate has gone. Nour's file shows A level papers passed last summer; Anis's shows O level papers and nothing since. Which file goes on the higher pile, and for what reason?

options.text: Anis's, because the O is short for Outstanding and beats an ordinary pass
Nour's, because the A is short for Advanced and those papers are sat later
Nour's, because the A is short for Average, and a safe pass is worth more
Anis's, because the O papers are sat two years after the A level papers

questions.explanation: The initial in front of the word level carries one piece of information and nothing else: which of the two examinations sits higher on the ladder. One opens the word Ordinary, the other the word Advanced, and a candidate reaches those advanced papers roughly two school years after the ordinary ones, so a file that holds them has climbed a step nobody can climb before the other. Neither letter is a mark won on a paper and neither hides a judgement on the person: a file that stops at the ordinary papers has simply stopped earlier, on the way from secondary school to a degree.

questions.prompt: A head teacher tells the staff how next year's money will go: "The school bus is our priority. The benches will be bought before anybody touches the roof, and the hall will be repainted only if there is anything left in June." Put the four items in the order they will be paid for.

options.text: the new benches
the school bus
the paint for the hall
the roof

questions.explanation: Three items are placed by sentences; one is placed by a single noun. Calling the bus the priority ranks it above everything else on the list, and that is the work that noun does: it does not tell you that the bus matters a great deal, it tells you that the bus is served first and dropped last if the year turns out tighter than expected. Read it as a warm way of saying important and the bus cannot be placed at all, since nothing else in the speech puts it ahead of the benches. The rest is built from what is said: one sentence sends the benches in ahead of the roof, and a condition that depends on what is still in the account sends the paint to the end of the queue, and perhaps out of the year altogether.

questions.prompt: A canteen manager rewrites her menu. She wants to be able to call the new one nutritious — that word and no other. Which change earns it?

options.text: lentils, brown bread and an orange replace a plate of chips
the portions are doubled and the same chips are served twice
salt and sugar are added, and the pupils empty their plates
the price is halved, so twice as many pupils can afford it

questions.explanation: This adjective judges one thing only: what the food carries for a growing body. It tells you nothing about how much of it there is, nothing about how it tastes and nothing about what it costs — which is exactly why the three other changes leave the word out of reach. Twice as much of the same plate is a bigger meal, not a better one; salt and sugar empty the plates faster and put nothing into the children; and a cheaper meal that feeds nobody properly is only a cheaper meal. Change what is on the plate and the word is earned.

questions.prompt: A ministry note on twelve village schools reports two figures for the year in which free lunches began: the number of pupils in class every day rose from 58 to 91, and the number of pupils who said they were hungry at noon fell. Which sentence reports both figures with the verbs of this lesson?

options.text: the lunches have reduced attendance and boosted hunger
the lunches have boosted hunger and boosted attendance
the lunches have boosted attendance and reduced hunger
the lunches have reduced hunger and reduced attendance

questions.explanation: These two verbs name a direction, never a verdict. One takes a figure upwards, the other brings it down, and the note holds one of each: the register climbs from fifty-eight to ninety-one while the count of hungry children drops. Hear put right in the first verb and you write that the lunches sent hunger up, which claims the children rose from the table hungrier than they sat down at it; hear the same thing in the second and you write that fewer pupils now come to school, which is the very figure the ministry is celebrating. Get the pair the wrong way round entirely and the note reads as a report of failure.

questions.prompt: A charity's full-page advertisement is ready: a headline in large letters at the top, a photograph beside it, a paragraph of figures underneath, and the postal address and web address at the foot. A reader says the page will move nobody, because the one line that could make him act is missing. Which line has to be added?

options.text: Nine children out of ten in the district never finish primary school.
Send twenty dinars this week, and one child eats every school day.
A FULL PLATE, A FULL CLASSROOM: THE ARITHMETIC OF A VILLAGE
Our association has worked in these villages since 1974.

questions.explanation: Take the page apart and you can name what it already has: a line in outsize letters across the head of the page, whose job is to stop the reader; a paragraph carrying the numbers and the years; and the two lines at the foot that say where the sender lives. What no part of that does is ask for anything, and a page that never asks gets nothing. The missing line is the one that hands the reader something to do and a size to do it in, which is what turns a page that informs into a page that persuades. A second slogan would only stop him twice, and another figure or another date would thicken a paragraph that is already full of them.
